Remand detainees

By: Joy Summers | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Weaponizing the criminal justice system to settle personal scores – its survival of the fittest as the SAPS investigating officers fail to do their jobs, and ordinary South Africans find themselves

Unique Selling Point:
powerful case studies with specifics that align despite not knowing each other

Summary:
We lost our lives – that is the common thread of some remand detainees whose family members or ex partners have used the criminal justice system as a means of revenge.
We speak to three unrelated case studies who found themselves in Pollsmoor, Westville Prison and Sun City – and all experienced a violation of their rights, the brutality of a dysfunctional system where your survival hinges on whether you have the means to bribe an official to make your life behind bars bearable. ‘you are not even a number, you are just a body they move from one place to the other’ says Muriel Robinson whose nephew accused her of assault The next thing the Douglasdale police rocked up and locked her away – all in she spent nine traumatic days behind bars at the Randburg court and later Sun City.
She is now effectively homeless with no money for a private lawyer and goes to court in September to try to prove her innocence. No investigation was done by the cops who shouldn’t even have had her arrested.


Further information:
A similar story is told down in Cape Town by Barbara Langridge who had a difficult relationship with her former business and life partner. She faced charges of kidnapping and extortion – which have now all been expunged and she is suing the state.
Craig Zaayman and his fiancée Marelize Sheekey were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit murder – they believe their ex’s got together – they lost everything and are beginning to rebuild their lives and are suing the state.

We will also speak to a former detective Manie Victor to find out how the cases should have been handled by the investigators.

Carte Blanche finds out more about this hidden shame of our criminal justice system, hold the officials responsible to account and brings to light a story that reveals that there is no safety net – if your accuser is malicious enough they can send you down the chute to hell – where you lose not only your rights but your life

Remand Restructure FINAL SCRIPT FOR TX SUNDAY 28th 2022 PART ONE AND PART 2

Voice over 1
An arrest is not meant to harass or intimidate, it should be a last resort. That is the theory, but not always the practice

Muriel
From when I got booked in at the police station, I was nothing more than a number maybe...otherwise I was an animal

Voice over 2
The stories are harrowing; people wrongfully arrested.. the power of the police used to settle personal scores

John Assor
Our law says innocent until proven guilty. I never, ever experienced that.

Voice over 3
It’s a journey that often ends in a maximum security prison, while your life on the outside falls apart

Barbara
They arrested me, I believe, without conducting a proper investigation

Fade to black

Voice over 4
Barbara Langridge owned a small art gallery in Cape Town, was a member of a civic association, and a treasurer of the local community policing forum.

Never having had a brush with the law, everything changed in February 2018

Up sound prison montage

Voice over 5
Barbara went to prison for a crime she didn’t commit

Barbara
There is everything that happened before this and everything that happened afterwards and in my two lives there is a definite line between the two that will never be forgotten

Voice over 6
What happened to Barbara could happen to you

Derek
What were you charged with?

Barbara
I was charged with kidnapping and extortion
Derek
But Barbara what evidence did they have?

Barbara
I don’t know, we have never been shown the police dockets we have never seen the statement.

Voice over 7
But she has her suspicions: at the time, she was in a personal dispute over a valuable property. She’s convinced this was the real reason behind her arrest

Barbara
The first thought I had was that it was a set up. The case was opened on the same day as they instigated legal proceedings at the high court to remove my name from title deed of a property

Link
You are meant to be innocent until proven guilty but your journey to hell begins out of sight in the cells of a police station – Barbara was first brought here to Milnerton

Voice over 8
Without so much as giving a statement, she was thrown into a filthy cell for the weekend

Barbara
There was no light, its completely dark in there you lose your sense of time and what have you

Voice over 8
It’s something another victim- who asked to be called only by her first name- knows all too well. Muriel was recently charged with common assault. She says it’s a trumped up allegation to get her out of the house she inherited, along with what she describes as a toxic and dysfunctional family

Muriel
I was the outsider and they had been trying to move me out of the house for several years

Voice over 9
She claims she was repeatedly provoked by a young male relative who cried assault when she knocked his arm away during an argument

Muriel
I don’t consider trying to swipe someone’s hand away assault.



Voice over 10
The police took her in for questioning, but Muriel says she was only ever asked her name, made to sign a notification of rights form, and was then locked up.

Muriel
I just felt very violated, I had come down to the police station under false pretences, that I was not being questioned I was just going to be put in a cell, and I just had this overwhelming thing that this can’t be happening.

Voice over 11
She remembers the squalor and the stench of the Randburg police cells where she says showers smelled like sewers

Muriel
Cigarette buts, chewing gum, sanitary towels shoved into the windows

Link
Wrongful arrests are common- and the amounts that you and I as taxpayers cough up in civil claims are eye watering but research shows most offending officers is slap on the wrist

Voice over 12
It’s unclear what if anything happened to the police who arrested John Assor.

John Assor
Other than being arrested and treated like a criminal, because that is how they treat you, they don’t listen to any reason

Voice over 13
He was accused of illegally pointing a firearm during an argument around a guesthouse sold by his fiancé. The buyer, businessman Thami Ndlala signed two agreements totalling R10 million rand. Once he settled the first R8 million, he wanted to move in- in violation of the agreements

Derek So the 2 million rand was outstanding and that's when things turned ugly?
Phia When Thami approached us one day and said the agreements don't work for me anymore. And that's when all hell broke loose.

Voice over 14
Thami Ndlala rented the property next door, and had started cutting down an interleading palisade fence. John Assor confronted him and their showdown was captured on this video

Derek
Thami, you wanted to take possession of the house for R8 million

Thami
As I was now the legal owner of the property
Derek
So John Assor came out, what happened?
Thami
And he wanted to be a man- let’s not forget in my property which was something I was not going to allow. He then went to fetch a gun- came waving a gun and I told my guys, to remain calm

Up sound video

Derek
This is a different story because the video shows nothing of a weapon being pointed.
Thami
What does the video show?
Derek
A lot of shouting and threats mainly from you
Thami
Mainly from me?

Voice over 14
John denies he was armed. Later Thami cut the gate locks, and stationed security guards with semi-automatic weapons around the property- he also cut the electricity

Derek
Why did you bring armed security guards onto the property?
Thami
It was to protect my asset. I brought an R8 million asset, which I had to ensure that I have adequate security for it.
Derek
I'd say it's quite a solid attempt at intimidation?
Thami
No they are not people that would require me to get security personnel to intimidate, I'm certainly not one that goes around intimidating people

Voice over 15
Then to John’s amazement the police from nearby Sophiatown arrived to arrest him on a charge of intimidation, assault and pointing a firearm

Phia
We were quite surprised when the police arrived there were literally about 25, 30 of them walking around Thami up the driveway.
Derek You believe that Thami used the police to strong arm you and John into leaving the property

Phia Well, that was pretty clear that that was his plan, to use the police, and they were really there in full force supporting whatever he wanted to achieve.

Voice over 16
That evening John says he was arrested without a warrant and thrown into the Sophiatown cells
Derek
Did they take a statement?
John
No, they refused. I specifically said to them that I had video evidence to show and prove my innocence and I would want them or expect them to at least look at it.

Voice over 17
The video did not save John from a night in the cells- but it would spare him from far worse. Next: Muriel and Barbara’s nightmare inside our brutal system was far from over

Barbara
And I was now going to Pollsmoor, I couldn’t actually believe it

Voice over
And things get tense in a heated discussion with Thami Ndlala

Derek
So you got a fact you don’t want to show us, you have a video you don’t want to show us

CUT TO COMMERCIAL BREAK END PART ONE 7 MIN 41

PART TWO FINAL

Voice over 1
Each year there are around 45 000 South Africans in maximum security prisons as remand detainees -waiting for a court date or bail. It can take up to two years. For Barbara Langridge that wait began in the cells under the Cape Town magistrates court.

Barbara
People have no shame they don’t mind urinating on the floor or worse, obviously getting tobacco is a big thing, getting drugs, the shouting, the swearing. I actually saw a police man beat up a woman in that cell.

Voice over 2
Her alleged crime involved a firearm, so her bail was denied

Derek
Do you own a gun?
Barbara
No. I've never owned a firearm in my entire life.



Voice over 3
But evidence didn’t seem to matter to the state. She was trapped in the system, now as a remand detainee, from a police cell to incarceration at Cape Town’s Pollsmoor prison, one of South Africa’s most notorious

Barbara
And I was now going to Pollsmoor I couldn't actually believe it. I just thought, this is...I never imagined in my life that I would be going there.

Voice over 4
Her time there began with an invasive body search

Barbara
Take them off! Anyway I stripped off, listened.. they said get on your haunches! And I had to hold the front of the booth with my hands up and you have to open your legs. And then they inspect everything.
Derek: The cavity search?
Barbara: Yes.
Derek: Must be the most degrading thing, I see you even put it in your little booklet here ?
Barbara
So exposed. I think that was possibly the worst thing I've ever been through in my entire life. So exposed and I am a very private person with my body, I don’t like showing it off

Voice over 5
Muriel’s charges related to domestic violence, which meant she couldn’t be released to her home address, so her bail was also denied. After two nights in a police cell she was on her way to Johannesburg’s maximum security prison, often called as Sun City. She felt like her world had ended

Muriel
It’s like someone pulled a blind down on my world. You’re just packed away in a box, everything just fades into this nothingness

Voice over 6
Both Muriel and Barbara were denied the very basics for a dignified existence

Barbara
So I didn't have anything to eat from and I didn't have anything to, you know, have a cup of tea. I didn't have a cup. I didn’t have a toothbrush but this young girl said would you like to use my toothbrush so I looked at the few bristles left on it and I thought I am just going to accept this help and I took it and she gave me some toothpaste and I brushed my teeth for the first time in three days

Voice over 7
Muriel used a tube of hand cream as a spoon.

Muriel
This is my cutlery set while I was in prison, it’s got a hard enough edge to cut pap, anything that I needed to go into my mouth this is what I used

Ema
You've got an influx of inmates constantly coming in and going out with a system that was never built for them in the first place.

Voice over 8
Emerentia Cupido is the spokesperson for The Judicial Inspectorate for correctional services. An oversight body of our prisons.

Emma Cupido
Emma: We are there to ensure that the human rights of those that are incarcerated are protected.

Voice over
But they admit they are powerless and can only advise

Ema
We have one of the best constitutions in the world. How do you have an oversight body that has no teeth?

Voice over 9
And remand detainees pay the price – behind bars and when they are finally released.

Barbara
The premise of innocent until proven guilty doesn't exist in the remand.

Voice over 10
After eight nights in Pollsmoor, Barbara was released on bail, she had lost everything. She closed the gallery, sold her car and possessions and – because the police kept promising evidence that never materialised - endured another nine court appearances over more than a year

Barbara
Everything I was before then was taken from me, being a business women, an artist, being who I was as human being

Voice over 11
A year later, the state suddenly withdrew all charges and expunged her record. Now she’s suing the police and the NPA.

The video saved John Assor because it showed he never wielded a firearm. He spent only one night in police cells. He too is preparing a case against the South African police



John
The prosecutor looked at the video and then decided that there was no case against me and they decided to pardon me.

Voice over 12
The Sophiatown police refused to comment. The provincial police have ignored our questions. Thami Ndlala meanwhile, promised us a different video that he says proves his allegations.

Derek
Why can’t you show it to us?
Thami
I didn’t come with that video here same way I didn’t come with all the eyewitnesses that were present that day
Derek
But not to bring video evidence if you have got it doesn’t make sense
Thami
I am not here to be on trial here
Derek
You are not on trial here!
Thami
I came here to deal with facts so me not coming ...
Derek
So you got a fact you don’t want to show us, you have a video you don’t want to show us
Thami
No I don’t have any...

Voice over 13
Despite promising to send us the video, he never did.

Voice over
The police won’t comment on Muriel’s case because it’s before court.

Last week she burned her prison clothes – a ritual performed by the remand detainees she met in prison.

Muriel
Somewhere between the actual law the police and the way the laws and the police act to mete out justice, our system fails. We have a wonderful constitution that means nothing !

Next month she must navigate her way through the court system she knows nothing about, with only legal aid as her guide- hoping that even as the police failed her, the courts will be where she can find truth and justice

THE END 14 01 DURATION 6 15



PROMO ONE 11 seconds
The stories are harrowing, people wrongfully arrested. It’s a journey that often ends in a maximum security prison, while your life on the outside falls apart

PROMO TWO 21 seconds
According to the law, remand detainees waiting for a court date are considered innocent until proven guilty, but thousands of citizens are incarcerated every year with fewer rights than convicted criminals

Muriel
It’s like someone pulled a blind down on my world. You’re just packed away in a box.

PROMO THREE
Voice over
From police cell to maximum security prison within days
Barbara
They arrested me, I believe, without conducting a proper investigation
Voice over
South Africans tell how a single malicious allegation landed them in prison
Muriel
And I just had this overwhelming thing that this can’t be happening
Voice over
Wrongful arrests are costing the state billions in claims

You’re just packed away in a box, everything just fades into this nothingness Voice over 6 Both Muriel and Barbara were denied the very basics for a dignified existence Barbara So I didn't have anything to eat from and I didn't have anything to, you know, have a cup of tea. I didn't have a cup. I didn’t have a toothbrush but this young girl said would you like to use my toothbrush so I looked at the few bristles left on it and I thought I am just going to accept this help and I took it and she gave me some toothpaste and I brushed my teeth for the first time in three days Voice over 7 Muriel used a tube of hand cream as a spoon. Muriel This is my cutlery set while I was in prison, it’s got a hard enough edge to cut pap, anything that I needed to go into my mouth this is what I used Ema You've got an influx of inmates constantly coming in and going out with a system that was never built for them in the first place. Voice over 8 Emerentia Cupido is the spokesperson for The Judicial Inspectorate for correctional services. An oversight body of our prisons. Emma Cupido Emma: We are there to ensure that the human rights of those that are incarcerated are protected. Voice over But they admit they are powerless and can only advise Ema We have one of the best constitutions in the world. How do you have an oversight body that has no teeth? Voice over 9 And remand detainees pay the price – behind bars and when they are finally released. Barbara The premise of innocent until proven guilty doesn't exist in the remand. Voice over 10 After eight nights in Pollsmoor, Barbara was released on bail, she had lost everything. She closed the gallery, sold her car and possessions and – because the police kept promising evidence that never materialised - endured another nine court appearances over more than a year Barbara Everything I was before then was taken from me, being a business women, an artist, being who I was as human being Voice over 11 A year later, the state suddenly withdrew all charges and expunged her record. Now she’s suing the police and the NPA. The video saved John Assor because it showed he never wielded a firearm. He spent only one night in police cells. He too is preparing a case against the South African police John The prosecutor looked at the video and then decided that there was no case against me and they decided to pardon me. Voice over 12 The Sophiatown police refused to comment. The provincial police have ignored our questions. Thami Ndlala meanwhile, promised us a different video that he says proves his allegations. Derek Why can’t you show it to us? Thami I didn’t come with that video here same way I didn’t come with all the eyewitnesses that were present that day Derek But not to bring video evidence if you have got it doesn’t make sense Thami I am not here to be on trial here Derek You are not on trial here! Thami I came here to deal with facts so me not coming ... Derek So you got a fact you don’t want to show us, you have a video you don’t want to show us Thami No I don’t have any... Voice over 13 Despite promising to send us the video, he never did. Voice over The police won’t comment on Muriel’s case because it’s before court. Last week she burned her prison clothes – a ritual performed by the remand detainees she met in prison. Muriel Somewhere between the actual law the police and the way the laws and the police act to mete out justice, our system fails. We have a wonderful constitution that means nothing ! Next month she must navigate her way through the court system she knows nothing about, with only legal aid as her guide- hoping that even as the police failed her, the courts will be where she can find truth and justice THE END 14 01 DURATION 6 15 PROMO ONE 11 seconds The stories are harrowing, people wrongfully arrested. It’s a journey that often ends in a maximum security prison, while your life on the outside falls apart PROMO TWO 21 seconds According to the law, remand detainees waiting for a court date are considered innocent until proven guilty, but thousands of citizens are incarcerated every year with fewer rights than convicted criminals Muriel It’s like someone pulled a blind down on my world. You’re just packed away in a box. PROMO THREE Voice over From police cell to maximum security prison within days Barbara They arrested me, I believe, without conducting a proper investigation Voice over South Africans tell how a single malicious allegation landed them in prison Muriel And I just had this overwhelming thing that this can’t be happening Voice over Wrongful arrests are costing the state billions in claims Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Remand detainees (6183 ) Joy Summers 29 August 2022

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Weaponizing the criminal justice system to settle personal scores – its survival of the fittest as the SAPS investigating officers fail to do their jobs, and ordinary South Africans find themselves
metadata.Unique Selling Point: powerful case studies with specifics that align despite not knowing each other
metadata.Summary: We lost our lives – that is the common thread of some remand detainees whose family members or ex partners have used the criminal justice system as a means of revenge. We speak to three unrelated case studies who found themselves in Pollsmoor, Westville Prison and Sun City – and all experienced a violation of their rights, the brutality of a dysfunctional system where your survival hinges on whether you have the means to bribe an official to make your life behind bars bearable. ‘you are not even a number, you are just a body they move from one place to the other’ says Muriel Robinson whose nephew accused her of assault The next thing the Douglasdale police rocked up and locked her away – all in she spent nine traumatic days behind bars at the Randburg court and later Sun City. She is now effectively homeless with no money for a private lawyer and goes to court in September to try to prove her innocence. No investigation was done by the cops who shouldn’t even have had her arrested.
metadata.Further information: A similar story is told down in Cape Town by Barbara Langridge who had a difficult relationship with her former business and life partner. She faced charges of kidnapping and extortion – which have now all been expunged and she is suing the state. Craig Zaayman and his fiancée Marelize Sheekey were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit murder – they believe their ex’s got together – they lost everything and are beginning to rebuild their lives and are suing the state. We will also speak to a former detective Manie Victor to find out how the cases should have been handled by the investigators. Carte Blanche finds out more about this hidden shame of our criminal justice system, hold the officials responsible to account and brings to light a story that reveals that there is no safety net – if your accuser is malicious enough they can send you down the chute to hell – where you lose not only your rights but your life
